newsitem.title: USA: Heinz says growth plan will boost stock.
newsitem.headline: Heinz says growth plan will boost stock.

text.p: H.J. Heinz Co's global growth plan, which calls for the company to become a global leader in six core businesses and post double-digit earnings growth, will produce stock appreciation over the next few years that will "richly reward" shareholders, said William Johnson, president and chief operating officer.

"A lot (of the appreciation) will depend on how well we do in developing the kinds of programs and initiatives to enhance our six strategies and to further operating profits and cash flow over the next three years," Johnson told Reuters.

"I think when you buy our stock people need to take a two-to-three year horizon...that's the horizon we're looking at...if you take that horizon I think people will be richly rewarded over that period of time."

Johnson also said the company is on track to post double-digit earnings growth in fiscal 1997, for which Wall Street's consensus estimate is $1.91 per share. The company posted earnings of $1.75 in fiscal 1996.
While declining to elaborate, Johnson, a 15-year Heinz veteran, said the company will make a "fairly significant presentation" to analysts in March.
"It will outline a program for enhancement of the stock, the share price and shareholder wealth for the next two or three years," he said.

Over the past two fiscal years, Heinz's stock price appreciated 52 percent during a period in which there was a secondary stock offering of nearly 21.8 million shares, a three-for-two stock split and two dividend increases.
"I don't think you'll see a 52 percent increase in the stock in the next 12 months," Johnson said. "I think over time (you will see stock appreciation."
"The executive vice presidents and me own far more than 100,000 shares each...so there is an enormous amount of attention and interest placed on this company."

About 15 to 20 percent of Heinz's stock is owned by management and workers. Heinz's strategic plan calls for the Pittsburgh food giant to focus on growing its six core businesses -- food service, which is the largest, infant foods, ketchup and condiments, pet food, tuna and weight control.
The company has been divesting businesses that do not fit the core units and is attempting to shed more, including poultry and ice cream businesses in New Zealand.
But Johnson said Heinz will not sell units for which it cannot fetch what it considers fair selling prices.

"These are not fire sales...we don't have to do it," he said. "If we don't get the price that we deem appropriate for these businesses, we won't sell them. They are profitable in their own right and the only reason we're exiting them is because they don't fit."
He said most targeted asset sales should be completed by the end of April.
"I won't give you a (sales) number because I don't know what it will be," he said. "It depends on what we end up selling."
